method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'Vulval and vaginal conditions' (Last updated November 2022), retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- each page carries '(c) 2026 The Royal Children's Hospital'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the 14 RCH guidelines and the Immunisation Handbook guidelines already in this compendium.

claims.claim: **Vulvovaginitis is common and usually resolves with simple measures.**
claims.source_text: Vulvovaginitis is common and will usually resolve with simple measures
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vulval and vaginal conditions' (Last updated November 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vulval_and_vaginal_conditions/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consider pinworms** when a prepubertal child has distressing nocturnal vaginal or perineal pain and/or itch.
claims.source_text: Pinworms should be considered when pre-pubertal children present with distressing nocturnal vaginal or perineal pain and/or itch
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vulval and vaginal conditions' (Last updated November 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vulval_and_vaginal_conditions/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Recurrent UTI symptoms with negative cultures: assess for vulvodynia.**
claims.source_text: Children with recurrent urinary tract infection symptoms but negative cultures should be assessed for vulvodynia
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vulval and vaginal conditions' (Last updated November 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vulval_and_vaginal_conditions/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Newborns** commonly have breast buds, white mucoid discharge, small vaginal blood loss and hymenal tags from maternal oestrogen; **bleeding in the first week of life needs no investigation or treatment.**
claims.source_text: Newborns are affected by maternal oestrogens crossing the placenta. It is common to have breast buds, mucoid white vaginal discharge, small volume vaginal blood loss and/or hymenal skin tags … Vaginal bleeding in the first week of life can be caused by the normal withdrawal of maternal oestrogens (requires no investigation or treatment)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vulval and vaginal conditions' (Last updated November 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vulval_and_vaginal_conditions/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Abnormal vaginal bleeding:** foreign body, excoriation (vulvovaginitis, lichen sclerosus, pinworms), trauma including straddle injury or **sexual abuse**, **precocious puberty** (secondary sexual characteristics under 8 years), urethral prolapse, rarely tumour.
claims.source_text: Abnormal vaginal bleeding in children may be caused by Vaginal foreign body (toilet paper, small toys or money) Excoriation due to moderate-to-severe vulvovaginitis, lichen sclerosus et atrophicus or pinworms Trauma, including straddle injuries or sexual abuse Precocious puberty (consider when secondary sexual characteristics <8 yo) Urethral prolapse … Tumour (rare)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vulval and vaginal conditions' (Last updated November 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vulval_and_vaginal_conditions/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consider whether a perineal examination is needed** and discuss with a senior clinician. **Examine once, by the most suitable clinician**, with a senior clinician supervising/chaperoning alongside the parent, after explanation and consent.
claims.source_text: Carefully consider the purpose / need for a perineal examination Discuss with a senior clinician If perineal examination is necessary, it should only be performed once, by the most suitable clinician Senior clinician should be present to supervise and/or chaperone along with the parent Provide explanation to the child and parent of the purpose of the examination and obtain consent
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vulval and vaginal conditions' (Last updated November 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vulval_and_vaginal_conditions/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Position:** supine or semi-supine on a parent's lap in frog-leg, or lying on the side with knees to chest.
claims.source_text: The perineum is best examined with the child supine (or semi-supine in a parent’s lap) in a frog-leg position: heels together, knees flexed and hips abducted; or lying on their side with knees drawn up to the chest
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vulval and vaginal conditions' (Last updated November 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vulval_and_vaginal_conditions/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Mild vulval erythema is normal before puberty.** Pale atrophic patches suggest lichen sclerosus; pain on cotton-bud touch approaching the peri-hymenal area suggests vulvodynia.
claims.source_text: Colour: erythema (it is normal for prepubertal children to have mild erythema of the vulva), pale atrophic patches (lichen sclerosis), bruising … Altered sensation or pain whilst progressively approaching the peri-hymenal area is suggestive of vulvodynia
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vulval and vaginal conditions' (Last updated November 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vulval_and_vaginal_conditions/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Document by describing, not interpreting**, findings. ⚠️ **Offensive discharge with bleeding before menarche suggests a vaginal foreign body.**
claims.source_text: Carefully document examination findings (describe appearance rather than interpreting findings) … Offensive vaginal discharge and bleeding in pre-menstrual children may be suggestive of foreign body in vagina
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vulval and vaginal conditions' (Last updated November 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vulval_and_vaginal_conditions/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Unclear cause or suspected vaginal foreign body: discuss with a gynaecologist.** Consider urine MCS.
claims.source_text: If the cause is not clear or if there is concern for a vaginal foreign body, discuss with gynaecologist Consider urine MCS
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vulval and vaginal conditions' (Last updated November 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vulval_and_vaginal_conditions/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Profuse or offensive discharge: swab for MCS at the introitus only** — no internal vaginal swabs.
claims.source_text: If profuse / offensive discharge: take a swab for MCS at the introitus (vaginal entrance), do not take internal vaginal swabs
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vulval and vaginal conditions' (Last updated November 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vulval_and_vaginal_conditions/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Features:** vulval discomfort, itch, dysuria, discharge, redness. **Causes:** thin, alkaline prepubertal mucosa; moisture, poor hygiene, irritants; pinworms, bacterial overgrowth, STI, foreign body. **Most need no investigations.**
claims.source_text: Vulvovaginitis Clinical features: vulval discomfort, itch, dysuria, discharge and redness … Thin vaginal mucosa (secondary to lack of oestrogen) More alkaline pH (pH 7) Environmental Moisture (synthetic fibre underwear, tight clothing, wet swimming costumes, obesity) Poor hygiene Irritants (soap residue, bubble baths, fabric softeners, antiseptics etc) Infection: Pinworms Bacterial overgrowth Sexually transmitted infections Foreign body In most cases no investigations are required
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vulval and vaginal conditions' (Last updated November 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vulval_and_vaginal_conditions/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Treat:** explanation and reassurance, remove environmental causes, good hygiene and vulval care, **vinegar baths (½ cup white vinegar in a shallow bath)**; low-dose steroid cream for severe itch or excoriation.
claims.source_text: Vulvovaginitis Clinical features: … Explanation / reassurance Avoid / address environmental causal factors above Encourage good hygiene and vulval care … Vinegar baths (add ½ cup white vinegar to a shallow bath and soak) Low dose steroid cream can be considered for severe itch/excoriation
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vulval and vaginal conditions' (Last updated November 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vulval_and_vaginal_conditions/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Pinworms: mebendazole 50 mg (over 6 months and 10 kg or less) or 100 mg (over 10 kg) orally as a single dose, repeated after 2 weeks**, and treat all household contacts.
claims.source_text: Pinworms Nocturnal vaginal shooting pain or itch Treat with mebendazole 50mg (> 6 months and ≤10 kg) or 100mg (>10 kg) oral single dose and repeat after 2 weeks Precautions to minimise spread including treatment of all household contacts
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vulval and vaginal conditions' (Last updated November 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vulval_and_vaginal_conditions/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Bacterial overgrowth** (e.g. group A streptococcus, *E. coli*) with significant erythema and pain: **consider cefalexin** per local antimicrobial guidelines.
claims.source_text: Bacterial overgrowth Significant erythema and pain caused by respiratory or enteric flora eg group A streptococci or E. coli Considertreatment with cefalexin. See Local antimicrobial guidelines
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vulval and vaginal conditions' (Last updated November 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vulval_and_vaginal_conditions/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Sexual abuse occasionally presents as vulvovaginitis.** Discuss persistent, recurrent or multiple presentations with gynaecology.
claims.source_text: Sexual abuse occasionally presents as vulvovaginitis and should be considered If persistent, recurrent or multiple presentations, discuss with gynaecology
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vulval and vaginal conditions' (Last updated November 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vulval_and_vaginal_conditions/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **A normal variant** developing from 3 months and resolving spontaneously by 6 to 8 years; usually asymptomatic.
claims.source_text: Labial adhesions (labial fusion) Normal variant which develops from 3 months (not present at birth) and resolves spontaneously by 6 to 8 years old when oestrogen levels increase at puberty … Usually asymptomatic
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vulval and vaginal conditions' (Last updated November 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vulval_and_vaginal_conditions/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **If the child voids easily, no treatment.** Oestrogen cream or manual separation are **not recommended** (high recurrence; separation is painful). **Outflow obstruction:** consider a short course of oestrogen cream after discussion with gynaecology.
claims.source_text: Provided the child is able to void easily, no treatment is needed … Other treatment options such as oestrogen creams or manual separation of adhesions (distressing and painful) have a high risk of recurrence, and are not recommended If there is urinary outflow obstruction, a short course of oestrogen cream may be considered, discuss with gynaecology
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vulval and vaginal conditions' (Last updated November 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vulval_and_vaginal_conditions/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Lichen sclerosus:** onset 5–7 years; itch, bleeding or discharge; pale atrophic patches. ⚠️ **Purpuric haemorrhage after scratching is occasionally mistaken for sexual abuse.**
claims.source_text: Lichen sclerosus et atrophicus Onset 5-7 years old, painless itch, bleeding or discharge; may be asymptomatic … Pale atrophic patches on labia and perineum, which may be confluent and extensive Scratching and other minor trauma may lead to further inflammation and purpuric haemorrhage into the skin. Occasionally this is mistaken for sexual abuse
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vulval and vaginal conditions' (Last updated November 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vulval_and_vaginal_conditions/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Lichen sclerosus treatment:** reassurance, avoid irritants, treat constipation, barrier ointments short term; **a course of high- then medium-potency topical steroid is often required — seek specialist advice.**
claims.source_text: Lichen sclerosus et atrophicus Onset … Provide reassurance Avoid irritants eg soap residue, bubble baths, antiseptics Treat secondary constipation Barrier ointments (eg paraffin, zinc paste) may help as a short-term measure Course of high potency (then medium potency) topical steroids is often required. Recommend specialist consultation
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vulval and vaginal conditions' (Last updated November 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vulval_and_vaginal_conditions/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Vulvodynia (pain 3 months or more without identifiable cause):** vulval care, pelvic floor physiotherapy, psychology if anxiety or depression, manage constipation; topical local anaesthetic short term only; **neuropathic agents (amitriptyline, gabapentin, pregabalin) only on specialist advice.**
claims.source_text: Vulvodynia Persistent pain in vulval area for ≥3 months without an identifiable cause … Vulval care is key Pelvic floor physiotherapy can be effective Psychologist input if associated anxiety or depression Ensure any constipation is appropriately managed Medications Topical creams with local anaesthetic agent for short term relief only Consult specialist (gynaecology or pain) for advice on suitability of agents for neuropathic pain eg amitriptyline, gabapentin or pregabalin
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vulval and vaginal conditions' (Last updated November 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vulval_and_vaginal_conditions/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Urethral prolapse:** chronic bleeding, pain, dysuria, straining; treat the precipitant (cough, constipation) and **refer to gynaecology** for topical oestrogen.
claims.source_text: Urethral prolapse Chronic onset, bleeding, pain, dysuria, constant need to strain Treat precipitant eg cough, constipation Refer to gynaecology for assessment and consideration of topical oestrogen cream
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vulval and vaginal conditions' (Last updated November 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vulval_and_vaginal_conditions/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consult gynaecology** if the diagnosis is unclear, advice is needed, or a foreign body needs removal. ⚠️ **Suspected sexual assault: follow local guidelines; early specialist consultation is vital.**
claims.source_text: Consider consultation with local gynaecology team when Diagnosis unclear Further management advice needed Removal of suspected foreign body If sexual assault is suspected, please refer to local guidelines. Early consultation with specialist services is vital
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vulval and vaginal conditions' (Last updated November 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vulval_and_vaginal_conditions/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Transfer** if a vaginal foreign body is suspected and examination under anaesthetic is not available locally. **Discharge** once diagnosed with follow-up in place.
claims.source_text: Consider transfer when Concern for vaginal foreign body and local services unable to perform examination under anaesthetic … Consider discharge when Diagnosis made and any required community follow-up is in place
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vulval and vaginal conditions' (Last updated November 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vulval_and_vaginal_conditions/, retrieved 2026-09-23
